requirement:
# REQ-2297: Add ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute to generated code.

Source: https://github.com/MessagePack-CSharp/MessagePack-CSharp/issues/2297

#### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.
MessagePack generated code is not decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.

Because it is very hard to write good coverage for generated MessagePack code, it may skew coverage numbers, especially on large projects with a lot of generated code.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
I would like all generated code to be decorated with ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute.  I do not feel like a setting is needed, but setting would be fine to have too.

#### Describe alternatives you've considered
There are no alternatives, it is close to impossible to write good coverage for generated code as it covers many edge cases.

#### Additional context

N/A

story.summary: The source generator templates for object formatters, string-key formatters, enum formatters, union formatters, the generated resolver and the composite resolver now emit `[global::System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]` on each generated type. The resolvers' nested `FormatterCache<T>` and `GetFormatterHelper` classes get it too. Every attribute is wrapped in `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK`. One shared helper (`TransformUtilities`) now writes a line break after `{` when a nesting type has constraints, so the new `#if` lands on its own line. The change adds a README note, a new test class with two tests, and 222 regenerated snapshot files.
story.why: REQ-2297 asks that all MessagePack-generated code carry ExcludeFromCodeCoverage so it does not skew coverage numbers.
touches_beyond_requirement: TransformUtilities.EmitNestingTypesAndNamespaces now writes "{\r\n" instead of "{" when the nesting type has constraints. This changes generated text for constrained generic nesting types. It is needed so the `#if` directive starts its own line.
README gains a paragraph that says the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 / .NET Framework.

The attribute is also added to the user-declared partial resolver classes (`GeneratedMessagePackResolver`, composite resolvers). These are the user's own types, which may be public, not only to new internal types.
story.confidence_overview: High that the templates and their compiled .cs files emit the attribute where shown, and that snapshots changed uniformly (S1, S2). Low confidence that the `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` guard is justified. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0, so those consumers (including Unity) get no exclusion at all. The new tests check that each generated file has at least one attribute and that every attribute is guarded. They do not check every type, and they never exercise the composite resolver.

refusals.what: The ExcludeFromCodeCoverage attribute is now emitted onto user-declared partial resolver classes, which may be public types of the user's assembly.
refusals.why: This changes the user's type metadata. It can break existing builds with CS0579 if the user already applied the attribute, and it is not configurable. The issue says a setting would be fine, so the owner should decide whether to add an opt-out.

refusals.what: The netstandard2.0/.NET Framework guard and its README justification rest on an incorrect claim about attribute availability.
refusals.why: The requirement asks for all generated code to be decorated. The guard silently exempts major targets, and the docs and test comment present this as a platform limitation.

Claim C12 disputed: Cited line CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs:18 states that ExcludeFromCodeCoverage is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework, and lines 82-97 enforce #if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK around every attribute; however, System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has existed since .NET Framework 4.0 and .NET Standard 2.0, so enforcing this guard prevents REQ-2297 from being satisfied on those targets.

Claim C14 disputed: README.md:1640 does not merely say the attribute is omitted on netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework; it inaccurately claims the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework ('only emitted for targets where it is available (not netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework)'), whereas System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has been available since .NET Framework 4.0 and .NET Standard 2.0.

The guard `#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK` rests on a false premise. System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute exists in .NET Framework 4.0+ and in netstandard2.0. Consumers targeting those frameworks, including Unity projects (a large MessagePack audience), get no coverage exclusion at all. So 'all generated code' is not decorated for them. The same guard is repeated in every template.

The README states that the attribute is not available on netstandard2.0 or .NET Framework. That is factually incorrect and documents the unnecessary limitation above. The test comment at CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs line 18 repeats the same claim.

The attribute is emitted on the user-declared partial resolver class. ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has AllowMultiple=false. A user who already put [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] on their own partial GeneratedMessagePackResolver (the natural workaround for this exact issue) now gets compile error CS0579 (duplicate attribute). The same applies to the composite resolver at CompositeResolverTemplate.tt line 8.

The test only checks that each generated file contains the attribute somewhere, not that every generated type has it. In the resolver file, removing the attribute from FormatterCache or GetFormatterHelper would still pass. `generated.Count >= 5` does not prove an enum formatter was generated, and the composite resolver template is not exercised by the new tests at all.

ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute has AllowMultiple = false. Emitting [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] directly on the user-declared partial resolver class (ResolverTemplate.tt:15, ResolverTemplate.cs:38) and partial composite resolver class (CompositeResolverTemplate.tt:8, CompositeResolverTemplate.cs:27) causes compile error CS0579 (Duplicate 'ExcludeFromCodeCoverage' attribute) for any project that already annotated its partial resolver class with [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] as a workaround, and also silently excludes any user-written methods or properties in other partial declarations of that class from code coverage.

All six templates guard [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] with '#if !NETSTANDARD2_0 && !NETFRAMEWORK' (and README.md:1640 and CodeCoverageExclusionTests.cs:18 claim the attribute does not exist there), but System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis.ExcludeFromCodeCoverageAttribute (without the .NET 5+ Justification property) has been available in mscorlib since .NET Framework 4.0 and in netstandard since .NET Standard 2.0. As a result, netstandard2.0 and .NET Framework builds still get no code-coverage exclusion on generated code.

In TestSource, MyEnum (lines 37-41) is never referenced by any [MessagePackObject] or [Union] type, while MyUnionMember (lines 48-53) is a second [MessagePackObject] alongside MyObject, MyStringKeyObject, IMyUnion, and GeneratedMessagePackResolver. Those 5 generated files satisfy Assert.True(generated.Count >= 5) (line 71) without exercising EnumTemplate at all, CompositeResolverTemplate is not tested in CodeCoverageExclusionTests, and RunGeneratorAsync (line 123) never verifies that the generated C# compiles without diagnostics.
